t: Replace All ?'s to Avoid Consecutive Repeating Characters - Three Candidates Always Suffice
o:
## Understanding the problem

Every `?` must be replaced by a lowercase letter so that the finished string has no two equal adjacent characters, while the original letters stay untouched. The input already guarantees that the fixed letters contain no adjacent duplicates, so only freshly filled characters can create a violation.

In `?zs` the `?` sits just before `z`, so any letter other than `z` is legal - the sample picks `azs`. In `ubv?w` the `?` is squeezed between `v` and `w`; 24 letters remain valid, e.g. `ubvaw`. The decisive counting fact: a `?` has at most two neighbors, hence at most two forbidden letters, while the alphabet offers 26 choices - so a legal replacement always exists, exactly as the statement promises.

With length at most 100 almost anything passes, but a single left-to-right greedy pass is the cleanest solution.
k: A `?` forbids at most the two letters adjacent to it, so some third letter of the 26-letter alphabet is always safe.
Filling `?`s left to right is sound: the left neighbor is already final, and the right neighbor is either fixed input or a wildcard handled later.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy Fill From a Three-Letter Candidate Pool
a.i: Scan left to right. For each `?`, try the letters a, b, c in order and take the first one differing from both neighbors. Three candidates always beat the two possible constraints, so the inner loop is constant-bounded and the whole method is one pass with no extra structures.
s: Copy the string into a mutable buffer.
Walk i from 0 to n-1, skipping characters that are not ?.
For each ?, test candidates a, b, c against the left and right neighbors.
Write the first candidate matching neither neighbor and continue.
a.t: O(n) - each ? tests at most three candidates against its two neighbors.
a.sp: O(n) - the character buffer (O(1) beyond the output).

a.n: Approach 2: Explicitly Ban the Neighbor Letters
a.i: Rather than assuming three candidates suffice, collect the actual set of forbidden letters - the existing left and right neighbors - then choose the alphabetically first letter outside that set. The logic generalizes unchanged to larger alphabets or wider neighborhoods, at the cost of building a tiny set per wildcard. Both approaches produce a lexicographically smallest completion when candidates are tried in alphabetical order.
s: Copy the string into a buffer.
For each ?, gather the left and right neighbor letters into a banned set.
Pick the smallest letter not in the banned set and write it into the slot.
a.t: O(26n) - each ? may scan the whole alphabet once.
a.sp: O(n) - output buffer plus O(alphabet) banned storage.

w: Either approach is interview-ready; prefer the three-candidate greedy for brevity and mention the banned-set version as the pattern that generalizes. Pitfalls: comparing against a neighboring `?` instead of a real letter (only ban actual letters), mutating an immutable string without copying first, and forgetting boundary positions where a neighbor does not exist. Edge cases: strings made entirely of `?`s and single-character inputs. Likely follow-ups: return the lexicographically smallest completion (the greedy above already does) or handle an alphabet of arbitrary size k.
